articles.title_orig: Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button
articles.title_zh: Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button
articles.content_orig:
Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.
Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.
The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.
The other big change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”
It’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s new AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.
This change says more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

NEW YORK, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Tumbling technology-related shares led a global stock sell off on Friday, with US traders searching for safe havens as the US 10-year yield dropped by the most in a month.
Traders ‌sold stocks in most markets with Japan and Korea down more than 5% overnight. Taiwanese shares were down 17% for the week, ‌their biggest weekly decline since 1990, while on Wall Street chip-maker shares fell 10.7% Friday and 17.1% for the week.
Anthropic, which debuted this week, fell as much as ​14.5% on its first full day of trading, just above its $83 IPO pricing, and ended down 9.1% at $88.30.
Consumer staples was the sole S&P 500 sector to end in the black on Friday.
"Markets are entering a more defensive phase," said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com.
"Strong AI demand and successful individual listings are no longer sufficient to sustain broader risk appetite when investors are questioning valuations, borrowing costs and the ‌outlook for corporate profitability."
The Dow Jones Industrial ⁠Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33; the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.39, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73.
MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe ⁠fell 34.89 points, or 3.30%, to 1,021.91. Its weekly decline of 8.1% was the largest since early 2020.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 2%, emerging market stocks fell 3.10% and MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan closed lower by 3.27%. Japan's Nikkei fell 5.06%.
The VIX index, linked to ​the cost ​of insurance against a drop in the S&P 500, closed at its highest ​since April 2025.
As investors sought safe-haven assets, government bonds ‌rallied.
The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes fell 10.43 basis points to 4.948%, the largest daily drop since October 22. The 30-year bond yield fell 6.81 basis points to 5.3329%. The 2-year note yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Federal Reserve, fell 13.21 basis points to 4.647% even as a rate hike is priced in for next month's policy meeting.
DOLLAR FLAT, OIL RISES LATE
The dollar index was little changed after touching a 19-month high on Thursday. The dollar's recent rally has been fueled by bets on ‌tighter monetary policy due to hotter-than-expected US inflation data.
"I think the momentum ​has stalled for the dollar ... but I think it's a little bit early to ​pick a top for the dollar," said Marc Chandler, ​chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets.
The dollar index fell 0.05% to 103.90, with the euro down ‌0.05% at $1.0961. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar weakened 0.67% ​to 158.6.
In commodities, crude prices ​rose late on Friday on worries about possible attacks in the US-Israeli war with Iran, and as traders bought crude ahead of next week's Thanksgiving holiday.
US crude rose 1.49% to $83.67 a barrel and Brent rose to $92.61 per barrel, up 0.68% on the ​day.
Gold prices fell to a 14-month low ‌after the largest weekly drop in 8 months.
Spot gold fell 2.81% to $3,520.09 an ounce and spot silver fell 4.22% ​to $40.95 an ounce. Copper declined 2.9% to $12,162.50 a ton.

articles.title_orig: State Department official accused of lavish ‘vacations on taxpayer dime,’ triggering travel crackdown: ‘Rubio is fed up’
articles.title_zh: State Department official accused of lavish ‘vacations on taxpayer dime,’ triggering travel crackdown: ‘Rubio is fed up’
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — A married couple nabbed cushy State Department jobs after hiring the realtor husband of a top White House official to find them a DC home — with the diplomat wife then taking questionable taxpayer-funded trips to Europe and Australia while allegedly boasting that she’s “never had so much free travel in my life,” sources told The Post.
Victoria and Zachary Roberts owe their roles to Office of Presidential Personnel (PPO) deputy director Morgan DeWitt-Snow, who led the State Department portfolio last year before assuming day-to-day control of the entire office.
Three sources told The Post that Victoria Roberts credited the couple’s relationship with Thomas Snow, DeWitt-Snow’s realtor spouse, with greasing the wheels of their hiring and say her subsequent globe-trotting amounts to “fun vacations on the taxpayer dime.”
“She traveled so much in such a short period of time it prompted the department to conduct a full audit of political travel and clamp down on travel writ large, which is a complete over-correction to one person’s abuse,” an administration official told The Post.
“Instead of punishing her — they won’t because she’s Morgan’s friend — everyone is punished and we are conducting less diplomacy as a result.”
The official recalled that “there was a political all-hands meeting a few months ago where they said that they are instituting a new policy for political travel to kind of clamp down on it. And she basically was laughing in the back of this room, being like, ‘Oh, that’s because of me, because I’ve been traveling so much.’
“But her travel hasn’t stopped,” this person added.
“It’s something that the senior State Department leadership, the people actually serious, are not happy about,” said a source close to the administration, adding that it was “demoralizing” for diplomatic staff to see people with “good credentials” get passed over in favor of the likes of Roberts, who the source called a “Tennessee bimbo.”
A person close to the State Department said “official travel is being abused and it’s usually being abused by these Morgan friends like Victoria Roberts. She went to Australia. She’s gone to nearly half of Europe. [Secretary of State Marco] Rubio is fed up with official travel .”
“There’s just this sense where there are way too many Morgan friends around in senior roles,” this source added. “It’s like, ‘Why are they here? What are they doing here? They’re dead weight.'”
The Robertses had no known relationship with DeWitt-Snow or Snow when they connected with the latter in February 2025. Victoria Roberts’ LinkedIn profile indicates she joined the State Department’s Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs (ECA) that April, the same month she and her husband signed the lease on a $3,750/month two-bedroom condo in Southwest Washington.
Zachary Roberts joined State about eight months after the lease was signed, transferring into the legislative affairs division from the Small Business Administration. In August, he was promoted to deputy assistant secretary for Senate affairs.
Victoria Roberts denied boasting of her extensive travel, telling The Post: “This is false, I have never said this.” The State Department confirmed that Victoria Roberts took an 11-day trip to Australia, with a stop in Hawaii, “to advance U.S. strategic interests in the Indo-Pacific, strengthen educational and cultural partnerships, and identify opportunities to better align… programming with regional security, economic development, and commercial diplomacy priorities.”
The department also confirmed a 10-day trip to Europe by Roberts, with stops in Germany, Greece, France, and the Czech Republic, to “advance U.S. public diplomacy priorities, strengthen educational and cultural partnerships, engage exchange program alumni, and ahead of America’s 250th anniversary.”
Both trips featured meetings with various local and US officials, and although the State Department says the trips were approved and included extensive on-the-ground work, a critic called the European swing “a thinly guised vacation.”
Asked if Roberts’ travel contributed to new department-wide restrictions on trips, a State Department official said in a statement: “While we don’t comment on purportedly leaked information, the State Department continuously evaluates its approval processes and implements changes as needed.”
The Office of Presidential Personnel plays an important role in both hiring and promotions, and Roberts has received two title improvements since joining, currently serving as deputy assistant secretary for academic programs.
Three people close to or inside the Trump administration told The Post that Victoria Roberts openly bragged that she got her position due to hiring Thomas Snow as her realtor — with one saying, “had she kept it quiet, I don’t think anyone would have put two and two together.”
Before becoming a high-ranking diplomat, Roberts worked as a spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Education and had no foreign policy or DC experience outside congressional internships.
“I asked her point-blank when I first met her how she got the job, and she told me without missing a beat that they hired Morgan DeWitt’s husband as a broker [and that] they did not know anyone when they got here,” one administration official told The Post.
“It’s been over a year now where they have been double-dealing, helping their friends, giving themselves promotions and title bumps … It’s a disgrace to this administration, and it’s a shame that it’s taken this long for it to be exposed.”
Two additional sources told The Post they heard Roberts credit both DeWitt-Snow and her husband for bringing her into the administration.
A person close to the administration said Victoria Roberts told them, “I didn’t think I would be in DC. I’m just from Tennessee, and I’ve never had so much free travel in my life.”
“She said tangentially, ‘Thank God for… the Snows, right?’” this source said. “She attributed it to ‘the Snows’.”
A person close to the State Department said of Roberts, “I heard her say ‘Thomas Snow’ when explaining how she joined the department.
“Let’s just say she’s not someone who’s the best when it comes to [operational security]. I think she would just go around saying that stuff,” this source said, clarifying that they “weren’t trying to pry” and the question is a normal ice-breaker in an administration where appointees often gain their jobs through relationships with other officials and people close to the president.
“Your nameless sources are spreading fake news about comments I never made,” Victoria Roberts said in a statement provided by the State Department.
A Trump administration official said that a February 2025 text message showed a third party introduced the Robertses to Thomas Snow while Victoria was setting up interviews in DC, arguing the couple’s decision to hire Snow and DeWitt-Snow’s decision to then hire them were unrelated.
“The New York Post was given evidence that confirm [sic] the two State Department political appointees referenced in this nonstory were connected to a DC-based realtor by a longtime mutual friend,” the official said. “As with the hiring of any State Department political appointee, proper vetting of qualified professionals is conducted by multiple officials in our agency to ensure the best candidates are selected on merit.”
A White House official added Friday in response to a request for comment that “Morgan Dewitt-Snow never interviewed Victoria Roberts. She interviewed with Cate Dillon, who is her current boss at the department and Austin Sprenger, White House Liaison. At the time, there was only one other appointee serving in ECA. Cate Dillon and Austin Sprenger cleared Victoria’s hiring through department leadership as they do with every other appointee at State, which at the time was Mike Needham and Dan Holler.”
Public records show that Thomas Snow has worked with other administration officials.
He was the buyer’s agent for EPA general counsel

articles.title_zh: 'They’re blowing this': Amazon's push against NYC delivery worker bill may be backfiring
articles.content_orig:
Published Nov 20, 2026 at 4:38 p.m. ET
Published Nov 20, 2026 at 4:38 p.m. ET

Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations
Amazon issued an ultimatum to New Yorkers on Thursday, warning its deliveries would get more expensive if lawmakers pass a bill forcing the company to hire many of its contract delivery workers as regular employees.
People across the five boroughs who opened their Amazon apps to order dish soap or dog treats were greeted by a new banner ad with the word “ATTENTION” bolded and highlighted in red.
“The NYC Council is considering Intro 518, legislation that could increase fees for New Yorkers by up to $5.00 per order,” the ad reads. “This bill would raise costs just when we need to make New York more affordable.”
But the move appears to be backfiring by antagonizing Council Speaker Julie Menin, who could soon bring the measure to a vote.
Menin, a moderate Democrat who is often viewed as an ally of the city’s business class, in recent days grew noticeably frustrated in her public statements as the e-retail giant ramped up its lobbying efforts against the bill, called the Delivery Protection Act .
“Amazon’s campaign is nothing short of a cynical ploy to trick New Yorkers,” Menin said at a press conference Thursday. “It is a last-ditch effort to try to escape the responsibility to the very workers and customers who have made the firm’s success possible.”
Supporters of the bill immediately cried foul.
Amazon used its app to urge New Yorkers to protest the Delivery Protection Act.
“Amazon is a multitrillion-dollar company,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani posted on social media . “If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it’s not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe. It's greed.”
“It's a bunch of BS,” said Queens Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, the measure’s lead sponsor. “We knew that they were getting desperate.”
The Delivery Protection Act would ban the third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver packages. Although most of the company’s delivery workers wear blue Amazon vests and drive Amazon-branded vans, they work for independent contractors called delivery service partners. There are more than 40 such companies in New York City, according to Amazon, employing about 5,000 people.
Amazon argues the system empowers small businesses and ensures packages are delivered quickly and at low cost. The company points to a study they helped fund that found the Delivery Protection Act would raise costs for customers by about $400 to $660 a year.
“As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written — which is why we’re doing this,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement. The company has threatened to move its warehouses out of New York City if the bill passes.
The banner ad Amazon put out on its app has an “Act Now” button where customers can send emails to city councilmembers. The company said its users sent about 20,000 messages within the first six hours of the campaign launch.
Supporters of the bill argue the measure won’t increase costs for customers, but would improve livelihoods for thousands of delivery workers. Delivery drivers organized by the Teamsters union say the system allows Amazon to escape liability for unsafe work conditions and faulty vehicles. Advocates on the City Council say the bill would force accountability by making Amazon hire its own drivers.
“ There's no world where this common-sense bill would cost Amazon $5 for every single delivery,” Cabán said in an interview. “This is just an example of corporate bullying. They want to bully New Yorkers with junk fees.”
City lobbying data shows the Five Borough Jobs Campaign, a group almost entirely funded by Amazon, has spent over $8 million this year opposing the bill.
The scorched-earth PR tactics echo another episode in New York City politics where a tech giant organized its users against proposed legislation.
In 2015, then-Mayor Bill de Blasio and members of the City Council tried to institute a cap limiting the number of for-hire vehicle licenses issued to companies like Uber and Lyft. Uber hired Bradley Tusk , a tech startup PR adviser and investor who managed Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s 2009 re-election campaign, to help sink the proposal.
Tusk describes in his book "The Fixer: My Adventures Saving Startups from Death by Politics," how he flooded the zone with negative TV, radio and digital ads while also ordering his team of lobbyists to “suffocate” individual councilmembers and their staffs. Similar to Amazon issuing a notice to its customers, Uber added a feature in New York known as “de Blasio view” to its app that told users to expect extensive wait times for a car if the legislation passed.
The strategy worked, and de Blasio pulled the bill before a vote. There were about 12,500 vehicles operating for Uber and Lyft in the five boroughs in 2015, according to city data. By 2019, the year lawmakers eventually capped for-hire vehicle licenses, that figure exceeded 86,000. The rapid growth of the e-hailing companies in New York correlated with more traffic congestion and the demise of the city’s yellow taxi industry.
In an interview with Gothamist, Tusk said while Amazon’s strategy may appear similar on the surface, the company was failing to deliver a credible message.
“Nobody believes that Amazon's going to stop delivering in New York,” he said. “So saying, ‘Oh, well, it might be a little more slower,’ or, ‘It might be a little more expensive’ — that doesn't move people.”
Tusk said that Menin could’ve been a sympathetic ear. Instead, he said the negative ads appeared to be driving her closer to politicians to her left, like Mamdani and Cabán, both members of the Democratic Socialists of America.
“Julie is no pushover,” Tusk said. “They’re blowing this.”
While supporters of the Delivery Protection Act like the Teamsters have called for an immediate vote on the bill, Menin has pumped the brakes, saying the legislation needs changes to address legal concerns.
Menin insists the changes won’t weaken the core intent of the bill, but protect it from potential legal challenges. A spokesperson for Cabán’s office said they expect the proposal to come to a vote by the end of the year.
“I have a very clear message for Amazon,” Menin said direct-to-camera during her Thursday press conference. “If you think that that is going to deceive New Yorkers and intimidate the City Council out of passing basic worker and consumer protections, you are dead wrong.”
Walter Wuthmann is a reporter covering public safety and the legal system.

articles.title_orig: Markets plunge: Nasdaq erases 2026 gains, S&P and Dow enter corrections
articles.title_zh: Markets plunge: Nasdaq erases 2026 gains, S&P and Dow enter corrections
articles.content_orig:
The surging stock market of 2026 capsized Friday, wiping out gains for the year in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite while the broad S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory, meaning they have declined 10% from recent peaks.
The dramatic sell-off is raising fresh fears about the viability of the AI investment wave that had powered stocks and economic growth for the first half of the year.
Friday’s declines were led by Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO just 24 hours earlier now feels like a blip after the stock lost 9%, wiping out hundreds of billions in paper wealth and putting shares just a few dollars above the IPO price.
Nvidia also dragged markets lower, tumbling about 14% following a Reuters report that regulators are looking into accounting irregularities at the chip giant.
With Friday’s losses of 3.7%, the S&P 500’s seven-day losing streak is its worst since the Covid pandemic; the index is now up less than 1% on the year.
The Nasdaq finished the day down 5.3%, and the Dow dropped 1.9%.
The losses also sully one of the most visible bright points of President Donald Trump’s second term. Amid sticky inflation and frozen housing and jobs markets, U.S. equities were the one part of the economy that appeared resilient. The AI investment boom created seemingly insatiable demand for stocks among investors, minting multiple new trillion-dollar companies in the process.
While Friday’s declines were stark, they were not sudden, capping instead a weekslong slide that began in early October as the combination of elevated oil prices , rising interest rates , mounting corporate debt loads , stubborn inflation , supply chain issues and a flagging consumer put increasing pressure on stock prices.
The sell-off picked up steam earlier this month in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victories, which raised fears of a slowdown in the tech sector’s data center buildout. Losses accelerated again last week as the scandal erupted involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and advanced chips potentially being diverted to China.
“The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth,” wrote Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, in a client note. “This has been exacerbated by the Nvidia crisis and the Democratic midterm win, which were a one-two punch for the AI story.”
Alongside the stock sell-off, investors have increased purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeking more reliable returns amid signs of weakening growth from higher interest rates and a stalling economy in China.
“The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday.
For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove nettlesome.
Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation.
“They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. Combined with a weeks-long downturn among AI and tech stocks, “we have dual forces hitting the market.”
A prolonged downturn could begin to cut more deeply into economic growth, he said.
“If you have enough of a protracted downturn, which we really haven’t had since 2007-2009 in terms of length and duration, that’s when you’d really start to worry,” he said.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock extends $2.5 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock extends $2.5 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell nearly 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.
The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $485 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ).
Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.
Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.
Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.
Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.
The sell-off spread across chip stocks , which had their worst week since 2001 , and the broader market.
Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report.
"Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.

articles.title_zh: Trump floats an unexpected name to be his successor as powerhouses Rubio and Vance stand by
articles.content_orig:
Chief of staff Stephen Miller praises President Trump's record on deregulation and the economy, and Trump jokingly asks if he wants to run for president.
During a lighthearted Friday afternoon moment with the media inside the White House press briefing room, President Donald Trump floated a new name to succeed him as president, while two expected 2028 hopefuls stood by.
The president asked the media if they'd like to continue with the press conference — where Trump provided updates on his trip to China where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This prompted laughs from Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who flanked him on either side during the briefing.
Then, he asked newly-minted Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, whom he called the "most powerful man in the world," to speak with members of the press.
MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028
President Donald Trump speaks as Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio look on during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Trump addressed the media after returning from a visit to China where he held trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
Miller took the podium and launched into a more than two-minute speech listing Trump's accomplishments from the first two years of his second term in office.
"I just wanted to say that what President Trump has achieved over the last two years is more than any president has achieved by far in American history. We can stand up here for four hours and go through achievement by achievement by achievement," Miller said.
He then rattled some of them off, including:
White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller speaks during a press briefing at the White House, Thursday, May 1, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
"Under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history," Miller said. "And I'm so proud to be his chief of staff to oversee on his behalf the staff in this building to keep delivering wins for this extraordinary American leader."
Trump was clearly impressed with Miller, who stepped in to replace Susie Wiles earlier this month following sweeping midterm losses for Republicans.
"We have breaking news! Breaking news!" Trump said. "He was better than these two guys," he added, turning towards Vance and Rubio, who both also spoke at the press conference.
"Do you want to run for president?" Trump asked Miller as he was leaving the podium, prompting laughter from the group.

No major names from either party have yet to announce their intentions to run for president in 2028 . But with the midterms finished, rumors have swirled about who will toss their hats in the ring.
Vance and Rubio are widely viewed as the two most viable options for Republicans.

articles.title_orig: Trump asks Stephen Miller: ‘Do you want to run for president?’
articles.title_zh: Trump asks Stephen Miller: ‘Do you want to run for president?’
articles.content_orig:
The president appeared to put Vance and Rubio through their paces as potential successors, though Stephen Miller unexpectedly stole the spotlight
“Which of you shall we say doth love us most?”
The ageing King Lear’s question to his daughters, expecting them to compete for his favour and carve up his kingdom, hovered in the White House press briefing room on Friday.
There at the lectern stood Donald “Lear” Trump. Behind him stood his potential heirs, JD “Goneril” Vance and Marco “Regan” Rubio, and to the side sat Trump’s favourite offspring, Stephen “Cordelia” Miller (more of him later). As for Lear’s Fool, the choices were endless.
Ostensibly this was a press conference to trumpet the president’s trip in Asia, but in practice everyone knew it was the first audition for the 2028 presidential election (and boy, is Trump going to enjoy turning the race into a contest for his approval). Vance is widely expected to seek the crown, though it was Rubio who came out on top in the latest Emerson College national poll .
In a jam-packed room, Trump stood centre stage as if hosting The Apprentice all over again. Behind him were the two contenders expressing their aspirations through matching suits, matching Maga red ties, matching US flag pins and matching leather shoes.
The first trial: could Vance and Rubio stand still for 90 minutes without rolling their eyes, yawning or silently mouthing “Kill me!” to the press? Could they force Trump’s word salad down their throats and look as if they were enjoying it? Even when the boss was rambling at length about potholes?
“When you fix a pothole”, began one detour by the octogenarian president. “I don’t want to bore you – they’ll say, oh, he rambled, he rambled terribly. I don’t ramble. I don’t ramble at all, but when you fix a pothole, you have brand new asphalt against old white asphalt that doesn’t look good, but at least you don’t ruin your car, but these roads were flawless …”
But first, the whole thing got off to a strange start. Trump appeared at the podium and remarked: “That’s a big, big a crowd. I’ve never seen this before,” but reporters crammed in the room could barely hear him above the whoosh of an air conditioning unit. An engineer tweaked the sound, but it only gave Trump’s voice an eerie echo.
Had the gremlins that grounded flights and frozen banking sites finally reached the White House? So much for America the hi-tech superpower. Eventually order was restored, though not necessarily in Trump’s brain.
He was evidently flattered by the media comparing his trilateral summit with the leaders of China and Russia to the Yalta meeting between Winston Churchill, Franklin Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin (he did not say which of the three he identified with, though critics could take a guess). Like a gushing teenager, Trump was so thrilled that Chinese president Xi Jinping had come to the airport to greet him, that he mentioned it twice (“He didn’t meet Sleepy Joe with the plane, that I can tell you.”)
The US, Russia and China hold 92% of global nuclear power, he noted, which gave him an excuse to bring up his uncle John Trump , an electrical engineer and former Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor. “A member of my family spent his life at MIT who they say is now the greatest professor in the history of MIT, so I have great understanding of- I guess maybe genetically I’m blessed,” Trump riffed.
At that remark Rubio could resist no longer. A smile spread across his lips and he shot a look at Vance, who felt obliged to smile back. We’re not laughing at you, we’re laughing with you, Mr President.
Indeed, Rubio had been the more fidgety of the pair. As Trump chuntered on, the secretary of state had shifted from foot to foot, fiddled with his tie, played with his lower lip, touched up his hair and given the odd wry smile. Vance, meanwhile, hid behind his beard and miasma of smugness.
But then, at last, came the moment for Lear’s daughters to make their public declarations of love. Vance went up the lectern and pointed out that he had stayed in Washington rather than joining the trip, comparing himself to Macaulay Culkin’s character in Home Alone – a child who is accidentally left behind at Christmas as his family rushes to catch a flight to Paris. “I missed you, sir,” he said to Trump, before praising the president for “securing historic trade deals” and reorganising the global economy to benefit the American worker and economy.
Not bad, but a little wonky. Marco, you’re up next. The secretary of state took aim at the critics who accused Trump of cosying up to dictators at the expense of Democrats, raising his eyebrows and shaking his fist: “These three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet. The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it’s dangerous.”
Trump began taking reporters’ questions. One young whippersnapper posed a question that will be asked many times over the next two years. “Because you have the vice-president, the secretary of state right behind you, I’m curious which of them do you think would make a better president after you?”
Trump swatted it aside without answering. Vance remained stony faced. Rubio smiled knowingly.
The same reporter put Vance in an uncomfortable spot by asking about his post-midterm tweet. “Would you argue that the war in Iran was worth it to lose the Senate?” The vice-president agreed with the goal of Iran not getting a nuclear weapon but added carefully: “I think the president is the one who makes the decision and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States.”
In other words, I hate this war and would never have started it but I have to back the boss. Expect a lot more of this needle-threading in the upcoming campaign.
Later, when Trump asked “Do you want to keep this going or not” amid a cacophony of shouted questions, he turned around to look at Rubio, who laughed, then at Vance, who did likewise with folded arms. The two rivals patted each other playfully. But neither was prepared for the man who would steal their thunder.
“We have the most powerful man in the world in the room right now,” said Trump, referring to Miller, the recently appointed White House chief of ideological zealotry, who stepped up to the lectern with bald pate gleaming under the bright lights.
“I just wanted to say that what President Trump has achieved over the last two years is more than any president has achieved by far in American history!” Miller roared , before offering the kind of vainglorious soliloquy that would make even a Kremlin or Chinese Communist party spokesperson blush. “What you’re going to see over the next two years, as astonishing as that has been under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history!”
Trump, who loves nothing more than flattery with exclamation marks, returned to the lectern and announced: “We have breaking news. We have breaking news.” Waving his hands, then with thumbs pointed at Vance and Rubio, he said of Miller: “He was better than these two guys. Do you want to run for president?”
That was a joke, right? Trump was stirring the succession pot again, making his potential heirs uncomfortable. It was fitting that he ended the press conference reminiscing about the night he hosted Ultimate Fighting Championship bouts on the White House South Lawn . He is going to relish every moment of presiding over a Republican cage match for the next two years.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Drops Below $150 Support After Jensen Huang Scandal: Key Levels to Watch
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Drops Below $150 Support After Jensen Huang Scandal: Key Levels to Watch
articles.content_orig:
The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis.
Nvidia shares tumbled 14% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang . The stock closed lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008.
Shares of Nvidia are down 46% over the period, pushing the company's market cap down by about $2.6 trillion. The stock is now trading at roughly 8.4 times forward earnings, while Advanced Micro Devices is valued at 29 times profit for the next 12 months.
On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further.
Once the most valuable company in the world, Nvidia now has a market cap of $3 trillion, putting it fourth behind Apple , Microsoft and Alphabet .
Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy.
Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."
But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD.
Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere.
On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this." In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December.
For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's $1 trillion plunge crystalizes the extraordinary power of a tech founder CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's $1 trillion plunge crystalizes the extraordinary power of a tech founder CEO
articles.content_orig:
Author of the AI Insider newsletter
It's rare that investors get a chance to put a clear dollar value on a CEO .
With Jensen Huang , we just got one. And it's an astonishing number: $1 trillion.
That's how much Nvidia has lost in market value since Huang was forced out of the AI chip giant last week.
It's potentially a terrible look for Nvidia's board of directors .
After all, the fundamental job of a public company's board is to look after the interests of shareholders. That doesn't mean maximizing the stock price every day, or keeping a CEO at all costs. Directors have broader legal duties and sometimes must make difficult decisions that hurt investors in the short term.
But when a board oversees the departure of a CEO and shareholders subsequently lose $1 trillion, it's reasonable to ask whether the directors have fulfilled their most important responsibility.
On November 11, the day before Nvidia announced Huang's departure, the company's shares closed at $173.73, giving it a market value of about $4.2 trillion.
By Friday afternoon, the stock had fallen to roughly $128, wiping out more than a quarter of Nvidia's market value.
According to Bloomberg data, the company's market capitalization has shrunk to about $3.14 trillion since Huang was ousted. That's a staggering $1.04 trillion decline in just over a week.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Of course, stock prices move for all sorts of reasons. And it's impossible to attribute every dollar of that decline to Huang's departure.
But here's what makes this particularly interesting.
Much of the bad news surrounding Nvidia was already out in the open before Huang left.
The original New York Times story about Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed and his relationship with Alice Huang was published in October 2025 — more than a year ago .
And the unconfirmed allegation that she might be a Chinese spy was reported on Oct. 29, a full two weeks before Huang's ouster.
Those worries had already pushed Nvidia shares down substantially.
Then Huang was gone early on Nov. 12. From that point on, Nvidia's share price became mostly a referendum on the man himself.
Suddenly investors were looking at something very different: Nvidia without the visionary founder who built it into the world's dominant AI chip company.
That's a particularly unsettling prospect in technology, where the person at the top can have an extraordinary influence on which products get built, which bets get made, and where an entire industry goes next.
Does Nvidia's board believe it acted in shareholders' best interests? How does it assess the enormous decline in market value since Huang left? I asked Nvidia's press office these questions on Friday and haven't got an answer yet.
There are plenty of ways to value a company. Revenue. Profits. Growth prospects.
But sometimes the market gives us a rare glimpse of something harder to measure: The value of one person.

articles.title_orig: European Union and UK strike a 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
articles.title_zh: European Union and UK strike a 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
articles.content_orig:
European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.
This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.
During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham said.
Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa said the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era.
He said jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction."
Burnham said that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances."
He went further and said " Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up new opportunities" for young people.
Von der Leyen said the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime."
She said the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers."
Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries.
She also said Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much."
Burnham said the agreements reached Friday, however, represent the most the UK could achieve at the moment, "What we are announcing today is probably ‌the limit of what we can achieve in this ‌Parliament, given what needs ‌to be done to implement it."
In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.
The three key agreements establish ways to:
The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements.
No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students
"There will be further discussions coming out of it on issues including on tuition fees," Burnham said.
Von der Leyen ‌said ⁠she was confident negotiators would reach a ​solution ​on ‌tuition fees, "We will be working ‌on that in ‌the ​next month and as we have a ​track record of finding ⁠solutions,."
On the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules.
They also agreed to link their emissions-trading systems, allowing them to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes.
According to the AFP news agency, London estimates the deal could boost the British economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually, and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation.
Leaders said they will establish a "structured dialogue on migration." Their joint summit statement said this would include "engagement with third countries" and "returns to third countries," among other issues.
The two sides agreed to launch formal talks on economic security and strengthen cooperation on export controls and supply chains, among other areas.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
On Monday, Burnham said it ​was the "obvious truth" that ‌Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit .
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave. In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

articles.title_orig: Feminist activist 'humiliated' after TV anchor reveals her relationship with network’s top executive
articles.title_zh: Feminist activist 'humiliated' after TV anchor reveals her relationship with network’s top executive
articles.content_orig:
A French feminist activist has gone viral over her furious reaction to a TV host who revealed during a live broadcast that she is the partner of a senior executive at the channel.
Anne-Cécile Mailfert was not impressed when an anchor introduced her as the partner of the second-in-command at France Télévisions, which runs public station franceinfo – all before she could speak a single word.
As the franceinfo anchor continued with the segment, Mailfert appeared dumbfounded and visibly enraged.
“So what?” she was heard saying in the now-viral footage. “Absolutely scandalous.”
Mailfert then turned to a male journalist on the panel and asked, “Who is your partner?”
According to The Sun , the activist was later seen stomping off the set before slamming the door on her way out.
The broadcaster initially defended their anchor’s introduction, saying it was in line with new rules around transparency and full disclosure.
By sharing the relationship status between its top exec and a guest panellist, they were preventing conflicts of interest within public broadcasters.
Despite initially arguing this, franceinfo later acknowledged that Mailfert should have been informed beforehand that her relationship was going to be mentioned in the package.
Yannick Letranchant, franceinfo’s head of ethics and transparency, said the station understood the tension between “necessary transparency” and the risk of “relegating an individual” to the status of being the partner of someone else.
Mailfert later addressed the incident on Instagram, saying she was deeply “humiliated” and “hurt” by what transpired.
“Yesterday, I experienced something that hurt me deeply,” she wrote in a statement written in French.
She insisted that she is “deeply committed” to the principles of “professional ethics, transparency, and integrity” but only if they pose a “genuine risk of a conflict of interest.”
“Many, if not all women know this experience: being reduced to their husband, their father, their boss, a man who is supposedly behind what they do,” she wrote.
She had the support of singer and former first lady of France, Carla Bruni, who is married to former president of France, Nicolas Sarkozy .
“Ever since I got married (at the age of 40 anyway) every journalist has reduced me to my husband,” Bruni wrote on social media. “Amazing and deeply sexist… Seems like I did nothing before him… You have all my support.”
Stay up on the very latest with Evening Update.
The controversy has also caught the attention of French politicians , including parliament speaker Yael Braun-Pivet.
“A woman holds her own convictions, fights her own battles, and speaks for herself. This should be a given in 2026,” Braun-Pivet said online.

articles.title_orig: Zscaler stock jumps 18% on report that CrowdStrike in talks to buy security vendor
articles.title_zh: Zscaler stock jumps 18% on report that CrowdStrike in talks to buy security vendor
articles.content_orig:
Zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor. Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%.
The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report. Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion. Zscaler, meanwhile, is down 13% this year, pushing its market cap down to about $32 billion.
Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era. Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap.
Should a deal take place, it would be among the largest in the history of the cybersecurity industry. Google acquired Wiz last year for $32 billion. In 2024, Cisco paid about $28 billion for Splunk. Earlier this year, Palo Alto closed its purchase of CyberArk for $25 billion .
CrowdStrike's deals to this point have been on the smaller side.The company announced plans earlier this month to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode.

articles.title_orig: Trump critiques Jensen Huang's replacement as he wades deeper into Nvidia turmoil
articles.title_zh: Trump critiques Jensen Huang's replacement as he wades deeper into Nvidia turmoil
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
President Trump on Friday offered a defense of ousted Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang, but — perhaps more significantly — criticized the new leadership of the chipmaker.
The comments came during a press conference in which the president again praised Huang's role in developing the company's advanced Blackwell chips.
"Jensen did that, and I think there are very few people in that company that can do that," the president said.
"I'm not trying to be disrespectful," Trump added of Huang's replacements. "I watched the people talking about how the company's going to be and where it's going to be." He didn't finish the thought, other than to say of Huang, "I would love to see him be back."
It was a clear reference to Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress and new board chair Harvey Jones, who took over last week following Huang's resignation and faced some criticism for their presentation on the company's earnings call earlier this week.
Kress took the reins of the company after Huang built close ties with the Trump administration. Huang was often seen in Washington at Trump's side or traveling with the president. He accompanied Trump to China earlier this year.
Huang resigned on Nov. 12 after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy as well as a direct subordinate amid questions about whether he oversaw the evasion of US export controls on advanced semiconductor chips.
Trump has noted Huang's desire to sell chips in China, but said he wants "only older chips" to be available.
"I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said on Friday. "We're a country of second chances."
Trump also showed support for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Friday, saying "I have not lost confidence" in his Cabinet member, whom he called "a different kind of a guy."
"He has a natural business instinct. I think he's done a very good job," Trump said.
Lutnick has been under fire for suggestions that he moved too slowly on the Trump administration's push to crack down on advanced chips from Nvidia and others making their way into Chinese hands.
Tom Cotton of Arkansas, a top Republican senator, told the Wall Street Journal Friday that Lutnick had repeatedly ignored warnings that US chips were being smuggled into China.
Cotton stopped short of saying Lutnick should be fired but declined to support him.
Both Lutnick and Huang are set to testify publicly before lawmakers in the weeks ahead in what could be two of Washington's most closely watched congressional grillings in years.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Wired headphones are making a major comeback — here are the best pairs to shop now
articles.title_zh: Wired headphones are making a major comeback — here are the best pairs to shop now
articles.content_orig:
NBC Selected independently determines what we cover and recommend. When you click on or buy through our links, we earn a commission. Learn more .
For most of the last decade, corded headphones have been nearly nonexistent. Phone makers dropped the headphone jack, AirPods became the go-to, and a tangle of wire hanging from your ears started to look dated. Now the cord is making a comeback.
After five straight years of falling sales, wired headphone purchases climbed sharply in the second half of 2025, according to the market research firm Circana , and revenue from the category was up about 20% in the first six weeks of 2026. The trend is visible, too: Wired earbuds have been showing up on TikTok and Instagram feeds and Bose released its first wired earbuds in 11 years this fall — and the first batch sold out quickly.
If you are interested in kicking it old school with a pair of wired headphones, keep reading, I’ve rounded up top-rated styles worth your consideration.
Every pick on this list connects with a cable. I included a mix of over-ear headphones, on-ear headphones and earbuds. I’ve included options that NBC Selected editors love, as well as highly rated options that have a minimum four-star average rating from one hundred or more shoppers.
If the wired comeback has an icon, it’s Apple’s white EarPods. More than 10,000 pairs sold on Amazon in the past month alone. I bought a pair recently after NBC Selected senior editor Nikki Brown mentioned she had switched back to using them because they’re affordable and less easy to lose. I’ve loved using them to make calls, listen to podcasts and more. When not in use, I love that I can wrap them around my phone.
The newest version uses a USB-C plug, so it works with the iPhone 15 and newer, plus most Android phones and laptops, without a dongle. Apple still sells lightning and 3.5mm versions, too. The sound is clear and pleasant and the open design lets in surrounding noise, which some people like for walking or biking around a busy city.
Bose launched these in October 2026, its first wired earbuds in 11 years. They connect over USB-C and an in-line remote handles volume, calls and noise-canceling modes. The only other earbuds on this list (besides EarPods), these come with three eartip sizes and two stability bands to help you find a secure fit. They’re also IPX4 sweat-resistant.
The ATH-M50x is a go-to studio headphone and it’s just as popular with everyday listeners because it delivers balanced sound. The foam ear cups keep your music in and outside noise out, which makes it practical for an office or a commute. And the detachable cables are a big selling point. Cords are the most common failure point on wired headphones, and with the M50x you can swap in a new one at no extra cost: . It  comes with three, including a coiled cable (for desks and studios) and a straight one (for on the go).
Koss introduced the Porta Pro in 1984, and it has barely changed since. The chunky foam earpads and metal headband look like they came straight from a Walkman ad, which has made them a favorite among people leaning into the retro side of the wired revival. Reviewers like bass-forward sound and value, and Koss backs them with a lifetime warranty. Just know that because the earcups are open, the people next to you will hear some of what you’re listening to.
If you’re a sound snob, these headphones from Sennheiser are worth considering. Reviewers call the crisp, clear sound of these “incredible,” and say they have “impressive clarity.” The over-ear design creates a spacious, natural sound, almost like listening to speakers in the room. They are also lightweight and velour ear pads keep you comfortable for hours-long wear.

articles.title_orig: How Carney’s Shift Toward China Could Become Leverage in Stalled U.S. Trade Talks
articles.title_zh: How Carney’s Shift Toward China Could Become Leverage in Stalled U.S. Trade Talks
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: Brazil ex-President Bolsonaro taken to hospital with abdominal pain, son says
articles.title_zh: Brazil ex-President Bolsonaro taken to hospital with abdominal pain, son says
articles.content_orig:
Brazil’s former president Jair Bolsonaro is back in the hospital for abdominal pain, according to his son Carlos Bolsonaro.
Jair Bolsonaro has been hospitalized repeatedly over the years for abdominal issues, after he was stabbed in the stomach on the campaign trail in 2018.
An ally of US President Donald Trump, he is currently under house arrest on medical grounds. Last year, he was given a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Carlos Bolsonaro said on Friday that his father was taken to the hospital again after experiencing “severe abdominal pain.”
“It was obvious that this moment would come, with an active man kept imprisoned, without having stolen a single cent from public coffers, under the pretext of a ‘coup plot,’” he posted to X.
Carlos Bolsonaro said his father has undergone more than nine surgeries after the 2018 stabbing and that his health had been deteriorating “every day” in captivity, citing his “lack of mobility and the psychological torture he suffers daily.”
He went on to say that he is the only one of Bolsonaro’s sons that the presiding judge has allowed to visit him, twice a week for two hours. He added that a request to stay with his father until further notice has been approved.
Upon arrival at the hospital, Carlos Bolsonaro said he was met with a “horrifying” sight.
“I’m with my dad in the initial room. The first impression was horrifying. Extremely severe abdominal distension, which is alarming,” he posted to X.
He said when he visited his father on Wednesday, the situation was very different and that everything seemed “normal.”
Tests revealed a “near-complete” intestinal obstruction, Carlos Bolsonaro added. He said his father is being given medication for pain and an “initial attempt to reverse the condition without the need for invasive intervention.”
“I’m sleeping with him and staying by his side right now,” he posted to X.
Jair Bolsonaro’s cardiologist Dr. Brasil Caiado said the former Brazilian leader underwent a scan that showed damage to his small intestine and signs of inflammation, according to CNN affiliate CNN Brasil.
Speaking to the press outside the hospital, the doctor said Jair Bolsonaro is clinically stable, medicated, conscious and calm, and will remain under observation for the next 24 hours, according to CNN Brasil.
Jair Bolsonaro’s latest hospitalization comes almost a month after one of his other sons, Flavio Bolsonaro, arrived in the US after fleeing Brazil following his defeat in the 2026 presidential election, in which he lost to leftist president Lula.
Flavio Bolsonaro vowed to lead his country’s opposition from the US and said he left his country to avoid imprisonment and censorship.
Concern from Bolsonaro’s party, Partido Liberal, came pouring in. “Once again, the aftereffects of the stabbing come to the surface and take a toll on the life of a leader who has been treated unjustly,” the party posted to X. “May God protect him, look after his health, and give him the strength to overcome this difficult moment.”
This is a developing story and will be updated.
CNN’s Marco Postigo Storel contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China takes centre stage at trilateral with US, Russia
articles.title_zh: China takes centre stage at trilateral with US, Russia
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.
