articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Loses Over A Quarter Of His Wealth After Scandal—As Google Passes Nvidia In Market Cap
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Loses Over A Quarter Of His Wealth After Scandal—As Google Passes Nvidia In Market Cap
articles.content_orig:
The 63-year-old billionaire's fortune stood at $131.8 billion as of Thursday, down $3.8 billion for the day, making him the world's second-biggest billionaire loser behind Japanese businessman Takemitsu Takizaki, according to Forbes' Real-Time Billionaires list.
He ranked 14th, behind Walmart heiress Alice Walton and ahead of Mexican billionaire Carlos Slim Helu and his family.
Huang was the world's eighth-richest person before trading began on Nov. 9, with an estimated net worth of $162.2 billion, a day after he admitted to having an extramarital affair. His fortune has since fallen nearly 19%, with several multibillion-dollar daily losses, the largest being $8.4 billion on Nov. 10.
Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, during the "Sferical One" event in Eric Ericsonhallen in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 15, 2026. Photo by TT News Agency via AFP
Huang owns more than 3.5% of Nvidia, making his estimated wealth highly sensitive to fluctuations in the chipmaker's share price.
Nvidia had lost approximately $800 billion in market value by Nov. 16 following the emergence of the scandal, Reuters reported, as investors weighed uncertainty over the company's leadership and future direction.
Huang resigned as Nvidia's president , CEO and a board member on Nov. 12. On Tuesday, he broke his silence for the first time since stepping down, acknowledging mistakes in his personal life and expressing willingness to return as Nvidia's CEO.
However, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones ruled out his reinstatement during the company's quarterly earnings call later that day, saying the board had unanimously accepted his resignation and would proceed with its search for a permanent successor.

articles.title_orig: Myanmar calls UN court's Rohingya genocide ruling a 'great disappointment'
articles.title_zh: Myanmar calls UN court's Rohingya genocide ruling a 'great disappointment'
articles.content_orig:
A Rohingya refugee waves Myanmar's national flag as he waits for the arrival of U.N. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman at a refugee camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 20, 2026.
The world’s top international court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority, more than a million of whom remain displaced.
The verdict , issued Thursday, is the first time a state has been found responsible for committing genocide in the history of the International Court of Justice, which was established in 1945. In a weekslong military campaign in 2017, Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 people, including up to 2,109 children under five, and forced more than 700,000 others to flee the country’s northern Rakhine State.
The landmark decision could have significant implications for the legal treatment of cases brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention, Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia Law School, tells TIME. That includes South Africa’s pending case alleging that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza , where Israeli forces have killed tens of thousands of people over the past three years.
A spokesperson for Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing told reporters on Friday that the ruling is “unfair.” Min Aung Hlaing was the military’s commander in chief during the 2017 operation.
“It was not a decision made unanimously,” spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said, pointing out that six of the 15 judges dissented. She did not say whether Myanmar would comply with the ruling.
Myanmar’s military junta-backed government denied committing genocide during the proceedings.
Read More: Myanmar’s Dictator Wants to Rebuild Ties With the West
The National Unity Government, a parallel government formed after Myanmar’s 2021 military coup, said on Thursday that it respects the judgment.
For the Rohingya, the ruling is “public acknowledgment in a court of law and in the top court in the world that what happened to them was genocide,” says O’Brien, who has published multiple books on genocide and international criminal law, is working on a book about the Genocide Convention in the ICJ.
Members of the Rohingya community also said the ruling is a historic recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group.
“Myanmar denies the existence of the Rohingya,” Sayed Ullah, a community leader at a refugee camp in Bangladesh, told the Associated Press , “but now the court made it clear.”
The court’s finding of genocide by a state is a historic first. Two previous genocide cases brought before the ICJ have gone to the merit stages, both arising from the wars that followed the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In 2007, the court ruled on a case brought by Bosnia against Serbia. The court determined that the killing of thousands of Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995 was genocide, but it found insufficient evidence to attribute the killings by Bosnian Serb forces to Serbia. Still, the court ruled that Serbia violated its obligation under the Genocide Convention by failing to use its influence over those forces to prevent genocide.
In the second case, which was brought by Croatia against Serbia, the court made no finding that genocide was committed. It instead ruled in a 2015 judgment that Yugoslav army and Serb forces had an intent to ethnically cleanse Croats from Serb-held areas of Croatia, forcing between 80,000 and 100,000 Croats and other non-Serbs to flee the Krajina region between April 1991 and April 1992.
“The Court has not rewritten or expanded the legal definition of genocide” since the earlier cases, Marko Milanovic, a professor of public international law at the University of Reading, said in a statement . “What it has done is take a more flexible approach to the evidence used to establish genocide, particularly the notoriously difficult question of proving genocidal intent.”
The dissenting judges argued that the evidence could support the intent of forced expulsion or collective punishment instead of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group.
The court ordered Myanmar’s military-backed government to ensure the safe, voluntary return of the Rohingya to the country and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.
Myanmar has two years to report to the ICJ on its orders of restitution. If it is unable to carry out restitution, the court ordered the government to pay reparations to the Rohingya, the amount of which will be determined at a later stage.
It’s uncertain whether Myanmar will implement the ruling, which is legally binding.
“Therein lies the rub in that there isn’t necessarily a mechanism for enforcing them,” says O’Brien. If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia, which brought the case to the ICJ, can turn to the United Nations Security Council, which has discretion over whether to act, although China, which has veto power as a member of the council, is friendly to the Myanmar government.
Third party states can also exert pressure on Myanmar to comply with the ruling, such as through direct diplomatic pressure or sanctions on individuals or companies linked to the genocide. On Thursday, the U.K. ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defense attaché and called for an urgent U.N. Security Council meeting to discuss the judgment. ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR), an independent group of current and former Southeast Asian parliamentarians, called on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to support implementation of the ruling. Cheah Wui Ling, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore’s faculty of law, says ASEAN is obligated to “act in ways that respect and not undermine” the ruling, given the organization’s commitment to international law.
Cheah says the ruling could give “fresh momentum” to efforts seeking to hold individuals criminally accountable for the genocide, including an investigation in Argentina and a criminal complaint in Indonesia .
The prosecutor at the International Criminal Court also requested an arrest warrant in 2024 for Min Aung Hlaing. The ruling could have a “snowball effect” on that investigation, says Vincent-Joël Proulx, an associate professor at National University of Singapore’s faculty of law and a former special adviser to the ICJ’s president.
Even so, other challenges remain to seeing restitution through, O’Brien says.
Nine years after the mass displacement, more than a million Rohingya refugees live in Bangladesh, with most in camps in Cox’s Bazar. Some refugees told the AP that they want to return home to Myanmar.
Read More: ‘There Is No Hope’: Death and Desperation Take Over the World’s Largest Refugee Camp
Rohingya refugees visit a market at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 17, 2026. Salahuddin Ahmed—AFP/Getty Images
But many of those homes and villages were completely destroyed, O’Brien says. “They have nothing physically to come back to.” She adds that the Rohingya have faced “decades of discrimination and persecution,” and it’s “very difficult to suddenly turn around a culture of hostility and discrimination.”
Restitution is “trying to put the victims in the position that they were in before this had happened,” says O’Brien. But “so many of them have lost family members, and so many of them have been subject to horrific violence and abuse, so they can’t be put in exactly the same position.”
Eyes are now on South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. The case is in a second round of written pleadings and is expected to take at least three more years.
Myanmar’s defense argued that its military operations targeted militants, not civilians. But the court considered a broader “pattern of conduct” by Myanmar, including hate speech, discriminatory laws, displacement, destruction of property, and widespread sexual violence.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
articles.title_zh: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
articles.content_orig:
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website , Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday .
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof 1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August , but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules , a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture , a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.content_orig:
Author of the AI Insider newsletter
It's rare that investors get a chance to put a clear dollar value on a CEO .
With Jensen Huang , we just got one. And it's an astonishing number: $1 trillion.
That's how much Nvidia has lost in market value since Huang was forced out of the AI chip giant last week.
It's potentially a terrible look for Nvidia's board of directors .
After all, the fundamental job of a public company's board is to look after the interests of shareholders. That doesn't mean maximizing the stock price every day, or keeping a CEO at all costs. Directors have broader legal duties and sometimes must make difficult decisions that hurt investors in the short term.
But when a board oversees the departure of a CEO and shareholders subsequently lose $1 trillion, it's reasonable to ask whether the directors have fulfilled their most important responsibility.
On November 11, the day before Nvidia announced Huang's departure, the company's shares closed at $173.73, giving it a market value of about $4.2 trillion.
By Friday afternoon, the stock had fallen to roughly $128, wiping out more than a quarter of Nvidia's market value.
According to Bloomberg data, the company's market capitalization has shrunk to about $3.14 trillion since Huang was ousted. That's a staggering $1.04 trillion decline in just over a week.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Of course, stock prices move for all sorts of reasons. And it's impossible to attribute every dollar of that decline to Huang's departure.
But here's what makes this particularly interesting.
Much of the bad news surrounding Nvidia was already out in the open before Huang left.
The original New York Times story about Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed and his relationship with Alice Huang was published in October 2025 — more than a year ago .
And the unconfirmed allegation that she might be a Chinese spy was reported on Oct. 29, a full two weeks before Huang's ouster.
Those worries had already pushed Nvidia shares down substantially.
Then Huang was gone early on Nov. 12. From that point on, Nvidia's share price became mostly a referendum on the man himself.
Suddenly investors were looking at something very different: Nvidia without the visionary founder who built it into the world's dominant AI chip company.
That's a particularly unsettling prospect in technology, where the person at the top can have an extraordinary influence on which products get built, which bets get made, and where an entire industry goes next.
Does Nvidia's board believe it acted in shareholders' best interests? How does it assess the enormous decline in market value since Huang left? I asked Nvidia's press office these questions on Friday and haven't got an answer yet.
There are plenty of ways to value a company. Revenue. Profits. Growth prospects.
But sometimes the market gives us a rare glimpse of something harder to measure: The value of one person.

articles.title_orig: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
articles.title_zh: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
articles.content_orig:
Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.
Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.
Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.
Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.
Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro . Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.
“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July .

articles.title_orig: Trump says Iran wants a deal, Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis exchange fire and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Trump says Iran wants a deal, Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis exchange fire and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund , was struck on Thursday in a Houthi attack in the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Iran-backed Yemeni group.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense said a Houthi attack on a tower in Riyadh’s financial center caused material damage to several floors of the building and nearby buildings, but no injuries were reported , state news agency SPA said. The statement did not identify the tower, but an accompanying photograph published by SPA showed the PIF Tower.
The Houthis said they had targeted Riyadh’s financial center twice on Thursday, first at dawn and again in the evening.
They also said they had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Khamis Mushait airbase in southern Saudi Arabia and SADAF Petrochemical Company in Jubail in the kingdom’s Eastern Province. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of these attacks.
The kingdom’s foreign ministry said it reserved the right to take “all necessary measures” to defend its sovereignty and protect its citizens and national assets following the Houthi attack.
The strike blew out windows across seven to eight floors of the PIF Tower, bending parts of its metal facade . It was the second time in less than two weeks that a Houthi attack damaged a landmark in Riyadh’s financial district, with state oil company Aramco’s building hit in a November 8 attack.
The King Abdullah Financial District was closed to visitors following the attack.
Three sources familiar with the matter said the building had been struck by an incoming Houthi missile . The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had “dealt with a missile threat” launched towards Riyadh and that debris had fallen.
PIF, which stands for the Public Investment Fund, acknowledged receiving a Reuters request for comment. The Houthis issued no immediate statement on the strike.
The Houthis have been firing at Saudi airports and oil infrastructure since Yemen’s frozen civil war reignited in July amid the US-Iran war. On the ground in Yemen, the group has seized swathes of territory from the Saudi-backed government, forcing it to stage a major retreat at the weekend.
Residents of the Saudi capital were awoken by a loud boom in the early hours of Thursday.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense issued several warnings of potential danger in Riyadh throughout Thursday, including after the attack, before announcing that the threat had passed.
The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported that Saudi aircraft had carried out airstrikes on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital Sanaa early on Thursday, without providing further details.
Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the strikes.
The conflict has dealt a blow to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plans to develop and diversify the economy of Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter and a US ally.
The prince met US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh on Wednesday, Cooper’s third publicly reported visit to Saudi Arabia since the Yemen conflict resumed.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that Saudi officials now foresee the campaign stretching on for up to six months , according to two Western officials briefed by the Saudis on the kingdom’s plans. A third ​source familiar with the Saudi plans confirmed the accounts.
The sources said the Saudis, who replaced the commander of their coalition fighting in Yemen this week, want to see their allies make gains on the ground before they enter any negotiations with the Houthis.
Meanwhile, the situation in Yemen has appeared to favour the Houthis, who have seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast including the strategically vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its mouth, and have surrounded the city of Taiz in highlands overlooking the government’s temporary capital Aden.
In the wider war, which began in February when the United States and Israel attacked Iran , there has been no sign of a breakthrough in negotiations mediated by Qatar.
Meanwhile, there has been an uptick in hostilities in the Gulf in recent days, with Iran firing at US allies Bahrain and Kuwait and US airstrikes hitting Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
Saudi Arabia first entered the Yemen conflict in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to restore Yemen’s government to power ​after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country. They fought to a bloody stalemate and in 2022 reached a ceasefire that lasted until summer this year.

articles.title_orig: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.title_zh: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.content_orig:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: Myanmar genocide judgment may bolster Gaza case against Israel
articles.title_zh: Myanmar genocide judgment may bolster Gaza case against Israel
articles.content_orig:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: ILO and China reaffirm commitment to South-South cooperation for decent work and social justice
articles.title_zh: ILO and China reaffirm commitment to South-South cooperation for decent work and social justice
articles.content_orig:
12th Joint Committee Meeting reviews progress and explores new opportunities to strengthen cooperation on employment, skills, social protection and emerging challenges in the world of work.
GENEVA (ILO News) – The International Labour Organization (ILO) and China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS) have reaffirmed their commitment to advancing decent work and social justice through South-South cooperation, with a focus on emerging labour-market challenges and partnerships across the Global South.
The commitment was highlighted at the 12th Joint Committee Meeting on ILO–China Cooperation, held in Geneva on 20 November 2026. The meeting reviewed progress since the previous Joint Committee Meeting in 2021 and explored opportunities to deepen cooperation.
The discussions took place against a backdrop of rapid technological change, persistent labour-market inequalities and the need to accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals.
Participants underscored the importance of translating development cooperation into practical improvements focusing on areas of longstanding cooperation including employment opportunities, skills and social protection.
Since 2021, China-supported ILO initiatives have contributed to strengthening institutional capacity, policy exchange and knowledge sharing, particularly across countries in the Asia-Pacific region.
Cooperation in skills development has supported training institutions and responses to growing demand for digital, green and industry-relevant skills. Employment initiatives have promoted high-quality and full employment, stronger public employment services, entrepreneurship and regional policy dialogue. In social protection, cooperation has supported efforts to expand coverage and improve service delivery, including through digital transformation.
Participants emphasized the importance of building on these achievements, sharing good practices and strengthening national institutions to ensure sustainable results.
Looking ahead, discussions explored how South-South cooperation could help countries navigate changes in the world of work, particularly those associated with artificial intelligence and the platform economy.
Participants considered opportunities to harness technological innovation for productivity and employment while addressing potential risks for workers and enterprises. They also highlighted the importance of connecting country-level initiatives with regional and global policy dialogue to broaden the impact of development cooperation.
The meeting further considered the role of the ILO–China partnership within wider development frameworks including the Global Development Initiative (GDI) and the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). China’s presidency of the BRICs in 2027 will also offer an important opportunity to advance cooperation on various world of work issues.
China has been a member of the ILO since its founding and has developed a longstanding partnership with the Organization. The ILO–China cooperation framework encompasses employment promotion, skills development, social protection, occupational safety and health, and South-South cooperation. Through technical cooperation, policy dialogue and knowledge exchange, the partnership supports countries in advancing decent work and meeting the Sustainable Development Goals.

China’s crude oil imports from the Persian Gulf surged by 42.4% in October from September, to the highest level since the Iran war began, as supply via the Strait of Hormuz rebounded and Gulf producers slashed prices for their crude to attract buyers amid record-high freight rates.
China imported 19.7 million tons of crude oil from the Persian Gulf producers, excluding Iran, in October, a 42.4% jump from the previous month, per calculations by the South China Morning Post based on Chinese customs data released on Friday.
October was the fourth consecutive month in which Chinese crude oil imports from the Gulf countries increased from the previous month, according to the data.
Gulf producers shipped almost half of total Chinese term supplies last month, at a level approaching the pre-war volumes, the estimates by the South China Morning Post showed.
The surge in Chinese imports from the Gulf coincided with the recovery of crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Additionally, Gulf producers reduced the prices of their crude grades loading for Asia as Hormuz flows rebounded and pressured down Middle Eastern crude benchmarks.
Rising supply from the Middle East has weakened both the Dubai and Murban prices. At the end October, the prices of physical Middle East crude slumped as flows from the region recovered and reached pre-war levels on some days.
Lower prices for December are expected to continue attracting buying interest in China, especially amid the slide in international crude oil prices.
Saudi oil giant Aramco earlier this month slashed the price for its flagship Arab Light crude for Asia for loading in December by $2 per barrel, to a discount of $6.50 per barrel to the Oman/Dubai average. This is the steepest discount for Saudi crude to the Middle East’s benchmark since May 2020 during the COVID pandemic.

articles.title_orig: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.title_zh: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has struck a deal on three policy areas with the United Kingdom in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
After a summit in Brussels on Friday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have concluded and a reset ⁠deal has been sealed.
“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe, and people across Europe and across the United Kingdom will get real benefit,” Burnham had told EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa at the start of the talks.
Downing Street said ‌both sides agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, ⁠and a link ⁠between their emissions trading systems. Details are due ⁠to be published ⁠in a ⁠joint statement.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done. Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation.
“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”
Burnham said the deals could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s economy.
The arrangement to reduce controls on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and EU is worth an estimated 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) to the British economy.
The agreement linking emissions trading systems will exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.
The youth mobility scheme will allow 100,000 young Europeans to live and work in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa.
Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations lie ahead for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.
Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation EU.
However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome and far from imminent.
That possibility and the agreements sealed so far will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains eurosceptic.
Nigel Farage, leader of the populist right-wing Reform UK party, called Burnham “naive” following the news of the agreements.
The EU has used this moment to “strong-arm the British prime minister”, he claimed. “It’s the same old game, and he’s fallen for it out of sheer inexperience,” Farage wrote on social media.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
articles.title_zh: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk," CNBC has learned.
Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, had built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5.
It's among the U.S. firms that have adopted Chinese models, whose usage has spiked across the globe this year, worrying lawmakers in Washington . The battle for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China has reached new heights in 2026 as Chinese models have improved.
But now Cursor plans to "explore phasing out PRC [People's Republic of China]-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk," according to a report produced by the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China, shared exclusively with CNBC ahead of its publication on Friday.
The report, which follows a months-long investigation into the adoption of Chinese AI models into the American tech stack, said Cursor "informed the Committees" of those plans. Airbnb and DoorDash also engaged with the investigation about their use of Chinese AI models.
SpaceX announced it entered into a formal agreement to buy Cursor in June; the deal was completed in August. SpaceX is developing the Grok family of models, which Cursor has been involved in training.
Cursor, SpaceX and DoorDash did not respond to a CNBC request for comment. Airbnb declined to comment. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The report found that cost, customization and near-frontier performance of Chinese AI models were driving adoption, with the U.S. lacking a competitive open-weight alternative at "price and performance the market demands."
"Beijing is now seeking to turn those technological gains into global market share and long-term dependence," the report says. China's embassy in the U.K. did not respond to a request for comment. China's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond.
It also sets out recommendations to address the issues it has identified.
Those include launching a "national American open-weight initiative" that combines public computing power, shared evaluation infrastructure and "lawful access" to American frontier models for training.
The report also says an order, made public in October, that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, should be built on, by prohibiting the use of "PRC-developed AI models" in federal information systems and in performance of federal contracts.
Separately, Washington is also concerned about Chinese companies accessing Nvidia chips remotely , via overseas data centers, and gaining ground by using " distillation ," where new models use older, more established ones to help train them.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.

articles.title_orig: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.title_zh: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.content_orig:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who was visiting Poland on Friday, said: "The impact of Russia's illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries." Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Friday's incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Nato scrambled jets on Friday after Poland said its airspace had been violated several times during a Russian attack on Ukraine.
Military aircraft were operating in Polish airspace while ground-based air defences were made ready , the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces said in a statement.
“These actions are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting Polish airspace, especially in areas adjacent to those under threat,” it added.
Poland earlier reported that three objects crossed over from Russia, likely including a KH-101 cruise missile, another missile and a drone.
Defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz condemned what he called a “provocation” from Moscow and said he would ask Nato for additional support on its eastern flank.
He assessed that it was unlikely to be a coincidence, occurring as Poland was set to hold military exercises of the 'Coalition of the Willing' of Ukraine's allies on Friday.
Russia’s foreign ministry says it will take ‘necessary measures’ after Estonia said it was closing its border with Russia.
The Baltic country's government said on Friday it would close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds from December 1 and will decide after six months whether to extend the suspension.
Estonia on Sunday accused Russian security services of staging an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defence company, in what it said was the second such incident this year.
Estonia's northern neighbour Finland shut its Russia border crossings in 2023, and has kept them closed since then, while southern Baltic nations Latvia and Lithuania maintain open crossings.
Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said on Friday that the incursions into Polish airspace do not look like an accident but an “intentional provocation” from Russia.
"We know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia,” he claimed in a press conference.
“Therefore — and this is not just my own assessment, but also that of our foreign partners, including those within NATO — it does not look like an accident. It appears that we are dealing with an intentional provocation.”
This week repeated Ukrainian strikes have seriously damaged the 19km (12-mile) Crimean Bridge, which straddles the Kerch Strait that links the Black and Azov seas.
The span is vital to sustaining Russia’s military operations, and the £3bn bridge is a potent reminder of Russia’s illegal annexation of the Crimean Peninsula, making it a prime target for Ukraine.
Train traffic stopped after the latest overnight strike into Thursday while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.
The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Putin as he met in China with Xi and Trump, as well as to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.
In China, Putin insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered it closed to carrying military hardware or ammunition.
Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” but vowed to rebuild it. The rail section, which runs parallel to the road, is believed to be stronger in order to bear the greater weight of cargo transport.
Ukraine’s defense ministry said the successful operation to target the bridge meant Russia would need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where “our drones are waiting for the cargo.”

In China, Trump called Putin “my friend.” The American president’s relationship with Zelensky has soured recently, although the question of US support for Ukraine could be raised by Democrats who will take control of Congress in January after their wins in the midterm elections.
European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy as they fear being sidelined by Trump’s direct talks with Putin.
Kushner said that, in his talks with Putin and Xi, Trump “sent a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”
He deferred to Trump on giving any details of the “private discussions,” but added: “I believe he also came away believing that peace is achievable and we need to all work together to try and achieve it.”
Putin said in Shenzhen that the Kremlin is not against European participation in talks, but “we need to understand with what Europe will come to these negotiations.” The Kremlin has proposed to European officials through diplomatic channels to come to Moscow “to determine their position,” Putin said, without elaborating. No date has been set.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to say which European officials had been invited or whether Moscow had received a response, Russian state news agency Tass reported.
Polish authorities were investigating reports that at least two unknown objects had come down near the border with Ukraine after the army said Polish airspace might have been violated during Russian strikes on Ukraine.
Authorities in Nato-member Poland said it was too early to say what the objects were. A Ukrainian air force spokesperson said it was likely that a Russian missile had crossed into Poland.
The Russian embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on Nato’s eastern flank since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, fuelling tension ⁠with the military alliance and stoking fears that the war could spread.
"We confirm the crash of an unidentified object in the village of Nowy Lipowiec," the district prosecutor's office in Lublin wrote on X. "Reports regarding potential additional objects in the region are currently being verified by the relevant services."
Footage shared on ‌social media from what appeared to be a security camera at a property in the nearby village of Chmielek showed an explosion in the distance.
Polish infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak said on X that a traffic controller had heard a loud bang near railway premises in Rudnik nad Sanem, about 50km west of Nowy Lipowiec. He said no visible damage to the railway had been found but that an inspection vehicle had been dispatched.
Klimczak also said air traffic controllers had been evacuated at the airport in Rzeszow, the largest city in southeastern Poland.
Prime minister Donald Tusk said he had received reports about security in ​the area and that there was currently no threat from the ‌air.
President Karol Nawrocki was ⁠also informed about the situation.

articles.title_orig: Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
articles.title_zh: Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
articles.content_orig:
The United States has pitched a new plan to secure post-war Ukraine when its almost five-year war with Russia finally comes to an end.
At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
Kushner’s comments came just hours after an unprecedented summit involving Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. At that meeting, Putin promised to retaliate against Ukraine’s attacks on Russia.
Following the Berlin summit, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov to push back.
Ryabokov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western ‌military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Ukraine applied to become a member of NATO in September 2022, seeking to fortify its borders with Russia.
But the Kremlin has repeatedly stated that Ukraine becoming a member of NATO would trigger “a harsh response” from Russia.
So could NATO-like security guarantees really work for Kyiv in light of Russia’s opposition?
European countries have been angered by the European Union being largely sidelined in the stop-start US negotiations with Russia and Ukraine since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi on Thursday has added to apprehension about whether the US president is serious about ending Russia’s war on Ukraine, particularly after his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his apparent recent overtures to Putin by relaxing sanctions on Russian oil.
But at a meeting of the “coalition of the willing”, a nearly 40-nation alliance of Ukraine’s European allies, in Berlin this week, Kushner and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff tried to reassure European leaders, telling them Trump had held discussions in Shenzhen on ending the war on Ukraine.
“Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side,” Kushner said.
“We do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential for ending the war,” he added.
Kushner also said Russia is “comfortable” with the idea of security guarantees for post-war Ukraine modelled on NATO’s Article 5, which says an attack on one member of the alliance is treated as an attack on all.
“I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” he said, adding that Trump was “open” to the idea but “obviously, it has to be in America’s interest” and part of “a broader security package”.
Kushner said Trump also called in to the Berlin talks after his meeting with Putin and the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week had produced no major breakthrough.
Described as the “cornerstone” of the military alliance, NATO’s collective defence principle, contained in Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty , was developed in 1949 to create a mutual protective pact to counter risks posed by the Soviet Union at the onset of the Cold War.
According to NATO, committing to Article 5 means that each member of the alliance knows that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.
That means that each NATO member is obligated to “take the actions it deems necessary to assist the ally attacked”.
When Article 5 is invoked, NATO allies are free to provide whatever form of aid and assistance is deemed “necessary to respond to the situation”.
However, it is not an automatic process. The article must be invoked and then agreed upon by NATO members and can take time to implement. First, there must be a meeting of the North Atlantic Council to assess whether the attack meets Article 5 criteria. Then there must be a unanimous political decision and declaration to invoke the article. This can be slowed down by deliberations, intelligence gathering and legal reviews.
After that, determining what is necessary to respond to a given situation is the individual obligation of each NATO ally and may not necessarily include military action. As NATO states: “It is therefore left to the judgement of each individual member country to determine how it will contribute.”
Each country consults with all other alliance members in terms of response and with the ultimate aim “to restore and maintain the security” of alliance members.
Article 5 has been invoked only once, after the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US by al-Qaeda.
The triggering of Article 5 saw “NATO engage actively in the fight against terrorism, launch its first operations outside the Euro-Atlantic area and begin a far-reaching transformation of its capabilities”, according to the alliance.
“By invoking Article 5, NATO members showed their solidarity toward the United States and condemned, in the strongest possible way, the terrorist attacks against the United States.”
Ukraine applied to become a NATO member seven months after Russia’s full-scale invasion began. Since then, Zelenskyy, his officials and Ukrainians around the world have been lobbying NATO nations to speed up Kyiv’s accession process.
But NATO members remain divided about offering Ukraine alliance membership during an ongoing war despite a broad consensus to signal strong support for Kyiv.
NATO members bordering Russia, such as Lithuania and Poland, have been most enthusiastic about backing Ukraine’s ambitions. Several other nations in the alliance have also been supportive of an expedited process for Kyiv to join despite concerns about corruption in Ukraine and while seeking an end to the war with Russia as a condition for the country to become a NATO member.
Under Trump, the US has been far less receptive to Ukraine’s calls for NATO membership. Indeed, Trump has publicly told Ukraine to give up its hopes of joining the alliance.
Yet last week, Kushner and Witkoff suggested that Kyiv could join the alliance in exchange for relinquishing eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region to Russia.
At the Berlin meeting on Thursday, French President Emmanuel Macron revisited the topic of Ukraine’s NATO membership. “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to NATO,” Macron said.
Also at the meeting, Kushner pitched NATO’s Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine without specifying how they would work.
This year, Zelenskyy stressed that for Ukraine, guarantees of security first need to come from the US. In October, the Ukrainian president and Witkoff discussed US security guarantees for Kyiv similar to Article 5.
But on Thursday, Zelenskyy told reporters that at the Berlin meeting, there was no common understanding of what Article 5-style security guarantees for Kyiv would entail.
He questioned whether giving Ukraine such security guarantees would mean that US and European troops would be based on Ukrainian land because that was his understanding of Article 5.
“For me, the most important thing is how countries will react on aggression,” he said.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director of geopolitics at the Rasmussen Global consultancy, who previously served on the NATO secretary-general’s policy planning staff, said there is inconsistency in US strategy.
“On one hand, they are proposing NATO membership to Ukraine in exchange for Kyiv entirely withdrawing its troops from the Donbas, and now they are saying Ukraine could get NATO-like security guarantees. It is clear Washington wants to show some kind of progress and get a peace deal done, also perhaps in light of the situation in Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.
